title: Tenerife 1977: The Crash That Changed How Pilots Talk

chapters.name: Intro
sentences: On a foggy afternoon in nineteen seventy-seven, two jumbo jets met on a single runway.
Neither plane was broken. Neither crew was new. Both aircraft were not even supposed to be at that airport.
Five hundred and eighty-three people lost their lives. It is still the deadliest accident in the history of aviation.
And the final link in the chain was not an engine, or a storm. It was a few unclear words on the radio.
This is the story of Tenerife, and of how it changed the way every pilot in the world speaks.

chapters.name: A Bomb on Another Island
sentences: The date was the twenty-seventh of March, nineteen seventy-seven. The place was the Canary Islands, off the coast of Africa.
Two Boeing seven forty-sevens were flying toward the island of Gran Canaria. One was Dutch. The other was American.
At a quarter past one in the afternoon, a bomb exploded inside the terminal at Gran Canaria airport. Eight people were injured.
There was a warning of a second bomb. So the airport was closed, and the incoming flights were sent somewhere else.
They were sent to a smaller airport on the next island. Its name was Los Rodeos, on Tenerife.

chapters.name: The Small Airport
sentences: Los Rodeos was not built for a day like this.
It had one runway. Beside it ran one main taxiway, joined to the runway by four short connecting roads.
It sat high on the island, more than two thousand feet above the sea. Clouds often drifted straight across the field.
And it had no ground radar. The controllers in the tower could only know where a plane was by looking out of the window, or by asking on the radio.
That afternoon, five large airliners were diverted there. They were parked wherever there was space, and they blocked the main taxiway.
So any plane that wanted to leave would have to taxi down the runway itself, turn around at the end, and take off the other way.

chapters.name: The Decision to Refuel
sentences: After a few hours, Gran Canaria opened again. The crews were tired, and they wanted to go.
The Dutch captain was one of his airline's most senior pilots. He was its chief flight instructor, with more than eleven thousand hours in the air.
He was also worried about time. Strict limits on working hours meant that a long delay could leave his crew, and his passengers, stuck overnight.
So he made a decision that seemed sensible. He would fill his tanks here, to save time at the next stop.
The refuelling took about thirty-five minutes. Fifty-five thousand five hundred litres went into the Dutch jet.
That choice mattered in three ways. The plane was now much heavier, so it needed more runway to get into the air.
The American jet was parked behind it, with only about twelve feet of space to pass. It could not leave until the Dutch jet moved.
And during those thirty-five minutes, the weather began to change.

chapters.name: The Fog Rolls In
sentences: At Los Rodeos, fog is really low cloud, blowing across the airport.
When the two jets finally started to move, the crews could see about five hundred metres.
Soon after, in places, it was less than one hundred.
The Dutch jet went first. It taxied down the whole length of the runway, turned around, and lined up for takeoff.
The American jet followed it onto the same runway. The tower told its crew to leave at the third exit, and wait on the taxiway.
The tower could not see either plane. The two crews could not see each other.

chapters.name: The Missed Exit
sentences: In the fog, the American crew counted the exits. One. Two.
But the third exit was a strange one. It pointed backward, and using it meant two very sharp turns for a huge aircraft.
A later study by airline pilots called that turn a practical impossibility.
The crew did not recognise it as their exit. They rolled past it, looking for the next one.
So the American jet was still on the runway, moving slowly through the cloud, straight toward the waiting Dutch jet.

chapters.name: A Few Unclear Words
sentences: At the end of the runway, the Dutch crew asked for their route clearance. That is the path to fly after takeoff. It is not permission to take off.
The tower read the route to them. The Dutch first officer read it back, and he added a few words. They sounded like: we are now at takeoff.
Did that mean waiting at the takeoff position? Or already rolling? The controller thought it meant waiting.
He answered: O K. Then, a moment later: stand by for takeoff, I will call you.
At that same moment, the American crew pressed their radio button too. They said: we are still taxiing down the runway.
Two radios, speaking at once, on one frequency. In the Dutch cockpit, the result was about three seconds of a loud, sharp noise.
The Dutch crew heard the word O K. They did not clearly hear the order to wait, or the warning from the other plane.
The Dutch jet was already moving.

chapters.name: The Runway
sentences: One person in the Dutch cockpit had a doubt. The flight engineer asked whether the American jet was clear of the runway.
The captain answered that it was. And the takeoff went on.
In the American jet, the captain saw landing lights coming out of the fog, about seven hundred metres away. He pushed the engines to full power and turned hard toward the grass.
The Dutch captain saw the other plane too. He pulled up early, so hard that the tail scraped along the runway.
The Dutch jet lifted off at about one hundred and forty knots. It was almost enough. But it was heavy with fuel.
It struck the top of the American jet, flew on for a short distance, and came down on the runway.
Everyone on the Dutch jet died. That was two hundred and forty-eight people.
On the American jet, three hundred and thirty-five people died. Sixty-one survived, most of them by climbing out onto the left wing.

chapters.name: Why It Happened
sentences: Spanish investigators found that the main cause was the Dutch captain taking off without clearance.
But they listed many other links in the chain. The bomb. The crowded airport. The fog. The radio noise. The missed exit. And phrases that were not standard, like we are now at takeoff, and O K.
Dutch investigators stressed that it was a misunderstanding on both sides.
And experts pointed to something else. Something human.
The captain was the most senior person on the flight deck, and a famous one. Two other trained people had small doubts. But they did not push hard enough to stop him.
No single mistake caused Tenerife. Remove any one link, and both planes fly home.

chapters.name: What Changed
sentences: After Tenerife, the language of flying was rewritten.
Today, controllers and pilots say the word takeoff at only one moment. When takeoff is actually being cleared, or cancelled. At every other time, they say departure.
A simple O K, or Roger, is not enough for an important instruction. The pilot must read it back, word for word.
And airlines began to teach a new skill, called crew resource management.
Its message is simple. The captain is in charge, but the captain can be wrong. Every crew member has the duty to speak up. And the captain has the duty to listen.
Tenerife received ground radar. And a second airport, in the sunnier south of the island, opened the following year.

chapters.name: Outro
sentences: The next time you fly, listen at the start of the flight, if you can hear the radio.
You will hear calm, short, exact phrases. The same words, in the same order, at every airport in the world.
That language is not a tradition. Much of it was written after one foggy afternoon in nineteen seventy-seven.
This video is in memory of the five hundred and eighty-three people who died at Tenerife.
